name: HotSpot Java ring-of-nodes mutation vs C at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C ring-of-nodes program (src/main/c/java_2_times_faster_than_c.c, malloc and free per node and per payload) built with gcc -O3; the README's 'Clang' row comes from build-clang.sh, which actually invokes gcc
workload: Build a ring of 10,000 nodes with a pseudo-random payload of 0-49 bytes, then run 1,000,000 mutations that each delete and insert up to 200 nodes; node count and checksum are identical in every implementation.
claimed_speedup: Java (HotSpot) 8.569 s vs GCC C 12.800 s and 'Clang' C 12.726 s (real time, one run each): about 1.5x faster than C (derived from page data). The project title claims 2x and the README dialogue says 'almost 2 times faster'; the measured ratio is about 1.5x.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm (build-gcc.sh); build-clang.sh also calls gcc -O3, not clang; compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source and target level 15, run as java -cp build/classes/java/main with default JVM flags (JDK build not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author's hypothesis: certain algorithms gain performance just from being expressed with automatic memory management, because the C version pays a malloc and a free per node and per payload while the JVM allocates and reclaims in bulk. The README adds that better memory management in C (issue #1) can beat the Java version.
tradeoffs: JVM needs a runtime and has higher memory use (not measured in the README). The C version could be sped up with a pool or arena allocator, which the author deliberately did not add.
caveats: One run per implementation measured with the shell 'time' (no variance). Compiler and JDK versions are not stated, and the 'Clang' row was built with gcc by build-clang.sh. Every new node and every mutation count calls sin() and fmod() through libm, so part of the gap is the libm cost shown in the second benchmark of the same repo (Java 51.2 s vs C 64.4 s for 1e9 calls). The author calls the title provocative, says it applies only to this algorithm, and notes that explicit memory management in C beats the Java version. Contributed Rust (13.824 s) and Go (14.542 s) were slower than C, C# (34.037 s) much slower.

name: HotSpot Java Math.sin/% loop vs C libm sin/fmod at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C loop calling libm sin() and fmod() (src/main/c/almost_pseudo_random.c) built with gcc -O3 -lm; the README's 'Clang' row again comes from a gcc build
workload: Sum fmod(sin(i * 100000.0) + 1.0, 1.0) for 1,000,000,000 iterations (a trigonometry-based pseudo-random function from The Book of Shaders).
claimed_speedup: Java 51.235 s vs GCC C 1 m 4.433 s and 'Clang' C 1 m 4.878 s (real time, one run each): about 1.26x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Contributed Go finished in 28.191 s (faster than both), Rust in 1 m 7.944 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm with no -ffast-math (build-gcc.sh); compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source level 15, default JVM flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author cannot fully explain it and lists hypotheses: HotSpot inlines aggressively after profiling, C math functions come from a library and cannot be inlined, and Java's % operator on doubles may map to better machine code.
tradeoffs: Measures the speed of the runtime's sin and floating-point remainder implementation against glibc's, not general code generation; JVM start-up and memory not compared.
caveats: One run per implementation (shell 'time'); compiler, glibc and JDK versions not stated, and gcc without -ffast-math or -fno-math-errno keeps libm calls for sin and fmod. The Java checksum prints as 4.9999999712235045E8 against 499999997.122350 for C (same value to the printed digits). Go, with slightly different floating-point results, was 2x faster than both, so the gap measures math-library cost rather than a language-level code-generation win.

name: HotSpot Java IntMap put latency vs C++ clang++ -O3: coralblocks/CoralBench
baseline: C++ IntMap (src/main/c/int_map.hpp, std::vector of std::vector<Entry> buckets) benchmarked with src/main/c/int_map_benchmark.cpp, built with clang++ 18.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -std=c++17
workload: Integer-keyed hash map put, get and remove: 3,000,000 measured operations per method, map capacity 1,000,000, warm-up 0, per-operation latency in nanoseconds from the repo's Bench class.
claimed_speedup: PUT average 31 ns (HotSpot with Graal JVMCI) and 32 ns (HotSpot with C2) vs C++ 48 ns: about 1.5x lower latency (derived from page data). GET is parity (27 ns and 29 ns vs C++ 26 ns). DEL is slower in Java (36 ns and 38 ns vs C++ 26 ns). GraalVM native-image: PUT 60 ns, GET 28 ns, DEL 50 ns.
compiler_and_flags: C++: Ubuntu clang 18.1.0, clang++ -O3 -march=native -flto -std=c++17 (the standard library is not stated; the code uses only std::vector). Java: Oracle GraalVM 25.0.4.1 HotSpot, java -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:NewSize=512m -XX:MaxNewSize=1024m (C2 run adds -XX:-UseJVMCICompiler).
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2288G @ 3.70GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.6 LTS, kernel 4.15.0-20-generic
tradeoffs: Java run needs a 4 GB pre-touched heap and a JVM. Worst-case PUT latency is higher in Java (maximum 211.7 us vs 18.4 us for C++), although the 99.9th-percentile maximum is lower (277 ns vs 1,040 ns).
caveats: The Java-vs-C++ section sits inside an HTML comment (<!-- ... -->) in the README source, so it does not render on github.com; a search-result snippet of a forum post describes it as published. Mixed result: Java wins PUT, ties GET and loses DEL, and the README text draws no speed conclusion. Not the same data structure: the README says the Java IntMap pools Entry objects to avoid garbage, while the C++ map uses vector buckets. One run per configuration with warm-up 0, so JIT compilation happens inside the measured region. No mechanism is stated for the PUT gap, so the tier is capped at C.

name: LuaJIT 2.1: print_to_file in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks
baseline: C fprintf loop (c/perf.c printfd: fprintf(f, "%ld %ld\n", i, i+1) to /dev/null) built with gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2
workload: Write 100,000 formatted lines to /dev/null; each language runs the benchmark 5 times internally, the Makefile invokes each script 3 times, and the overall minimum is reported.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 6.26 ms vs C 8.02 ms (0.78x of the C time, about 1.28x faster, derived from page data). Rust 4.17 ms (0.52x) is also faster than C; Julia 10.17 ms (1.27x) and Java 58.74 ms are slower.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2 (the Makefile builds benchmarks/c.csv from the -O2 binary, not -O3), linked with OpenBLAS; LuaJIT 2.1.1703358377 run as 'luajit lua/perf.lua'.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (x86_64); CPU model not stated; single-threaded environment variables set
tradeoffs: The win covers formatted integer output only; LuaJIT needs its runtime and the result excludes start-up.
caveats: Only 1 of the 8 benchmarks goes LuaJIT's way; it is slower than C on the other seven (recursion_fibonacci 5.20x, userfunc_mandelbrot 2.54x, matrix_statistics 2.29x, recursion_quicksort 2.24x, iteration_pi_sum 1.07x, parse_integers 1.21x, matrix_multiply 1.14x). Times are milliseconds measured on a shared CI runner with no CPU model, C built at -O2 not -O3, and the C side's time is dominated by glibc vfprintf, so the gap most likely reflects LuaJIT's own number formatting against glibc (inference; the source states no mechanism, which caps the tier at C). Not a language-level code-generation win.

name: OpenJDK 25 HotSpot: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: Java (OpenJDK 25.0.4) 0.347 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 2.9x faster than C and 3.3x faster than C++ (derived from page data). C# 0.931 s, OCaml 0.865 s and Nim 0.809 s also beat C on this workload.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins). Java: OpenJDK 25.0.4, javac bench.java then java bench (default heap, default GC).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 987.8 MiB for Java vs 33.3 MiB for C (all five workloads in one process); JVM start-up and warm-up are inside the timed region.
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free; an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. The benchmark is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs Java 13.536 s, C# 11.914 s, OCaml 16.233 s; C is faster on Fibonacci, strings and, for Java and OCaml, primes). Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT warm-up inside the timed region and may use extra GC and JIT threads, so wall time is not CPU time. The Java program lets nodes become garbage without any explicit free, which is the point of the comparison but not equivalent memory management.

name: Julia 1.6 density-gradient kernel vs C++ at g++ -O3: zyth0s/bench_density_gradient_wfn
baseline: C++ port of the same density-gradient routine (cpp/lib.cpp using std::valarray, called through ccall) built with g++ -Wall --std=c++11 -O3 -march=native -fPIC -funroll-loops; the README lists 'g++' as Apple clang 11.0.3
workload: Evaluate the electron-density gradient of a wavefunction at one point, 10 evaluations per sample, for CH4, C2H4 and imidazol (BenchmarkTools timings).
claimed_speedup: imidazol: Julia 112.843 us vs C++ 123.619 us; C2H4: Julia 41.737 us vs C++ 45.770 us (each about 9% faster, derived from page data). CH4: Julia 20.021 us vs C++ 19.656 us (C++ about 2% faster). Fortran (66.975 us on imidazol) and Rust (109.139 us) beat Julia.
compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ (Apple clang version 11.0.3) --std=c++11 -O3 -march=native -fPIC -funroll-loops, Eigen headers vendored; Julia 1.6.0 (LLVM 11.0.1) with -O3 -C skylake --check-bounds=no, StaticArrays, @views and @inbounds, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=1.
tradeoffs: Julia allocates more (122 to 202 allocations, 14-27 KiB per call) than the C++ and Fortran versions (2 allocations, 224 bytes) and needs the JIT warm-up that BenchmarkTools excludes.
caveats: Small margin (about 9%) on two of three inputs and a loss on the smallest; the author says Fortran is fastest and Rust beats Julia on the larger inputs, and calls the C++ valarray version 'tedious', so the C++ port may be under-optimised. The compiler is Apple clang, not GNU g++. One BenchmarkTools result per case; no mechanism is given for Julia scaling better than C++ and Rust, so the tier is capped at C. The repo has not been updated since 2021.
